title: Serving LLMs on Kubernetes: Why Round-Robin Breaks and What Replaces It
excerpt: KV-cache pressure, prefix caching and the Gateway API Inference Extension — how model-aware routing is replacing classic load balancing for LLM traffic.
content:
## Round-robin works until the requests are LLM prompts

Classic load balancing assumes requests are roughly the same size. Round-robin or least-connections across a pool of replicas is good enough for a REST API where every call takes a few milliseconds.

LLM inference breaks that assumption completely:

- one request is a 20-token question, the next is a 30,000-token document with a 2,000-token answer;
- each replica holds a **KV cache** of attention state for in-flight sequences, and its free space decides how many requests it can batch;
- replicas that already hold a prompt prefix in cache (a shared system prompt, a long chat history) can skip most of the prefill work for follow-up requests.

Send a long prompt to a replica whose KV cache is nearly full and it queues; send a follow-up turn to a replica that doesn't have the conversation cached and you redo all the prefill. A load balancer that can't see these signals leaves a lot of GPU on the table.

---

## 1. What the serving engine does

Engines such as **vLLM** made high-throughput serving practical with ideas like **PagedAttention** (managing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual memory pages), **continuous batching** (adding and removing sequences from a running batch every step) and **prefix caching** (reusing cached blocks for identical prompt prefixes).

These engines expose exactly the metrics a smarter router needs: queue depth, running requests, KV-cache utilisation, and which adapters are loaded.

---

## 2. Model-aware routing on Kubernetes

The Kubernetes community's response is the **Gateway API Inference Extension**. It adds an `InferencePool` resource (a set of model-server pods) and an **endpoint picker** that the gateway consults for every request. Instead of round-robin, the picker scores replicas on live serving metrics:

```text
 client ──► Gateway (Envoy) ──► Endpoint Picker ──► best replica
                                 │  scores using:
                                 │   • queue length
                                 │   • KV-cache utilisation
                                 │   • prefix-cache affinity
                                 │   • loaded LoRA adapters
                                 ▼
                       [ vLLM pod ] [ vLLM pod ] [ vLLM pod ]
```

Projects like **llm-d** build on this with prefix-cache-aware routing and **disaggregated serving** — running the compute-heavy *prefill* phase and the memory-bandwidth-heavy *decode* phase on separate pools that can be scaled independently.

---

## 3. A scoring function, simplified

The core idea fits in a few lines. This is a simplified version of the kind of scorer an endpoint picker runs — not any project's exact algorithm:

```go
type Replica struct {
    Name          string
    QueueLen      int     // requests waiting
    KVUtil        float64 // 0.0 - 1.0
    HasPrefix     bool    // prompt prefix already cached here
    HasAdapter    bool    // requested LoRA adapter loaded
}

func score(r Replica) float64 {
    if r.KVUtil > 0.95 {
        return -1 // effectively full: avoid unless nothing else
    }
    s := 1.0 - r.KVUtil            // headroom to batch more work
    s -= 0.15 * float64(r.QueueLen) // penalise waiting requests
    if r.HasPrefix {
        s += 0.5 // skipping prefill is a big win
    }
    if r.HasAdapter {
        s += 0.3 // avoids an adapter swap
    }
    return s
}

func pick(replicas []Replica) Replica {
    best := replicas[0]
    for _, r := range replicas[1:] {
        if score(r) > score(best) {
            best = r
        }
    }
    return best
}
```

The weights are where the engineering lives: too much prefix affinity and one hot replica melts while others idle; too little and you throw away cache hits. Production systems tune these against real traffic and fall back to plain load balancing when metrics go stale.

---

## 4. What I learned serving models myself

Building Lyra — a vocal studio that runs diffusion-based voice conversion — taught me the same lesson at small scale. GPU work is lumpy: a 10-second take and a 4-minute song are not the same request. Things that mattered most:

- **Admission control before routing.** Rejecting or queueing work early beats letting a worker run out of memory halfway through.
- **Make jobs resumable.** Long renders must survive dropped connections; clients should reconnect to a job, not restart it.
- **Expose the right metrics.** Queue length and memory headroom are more useful than CPU percentage for anything on a GPU.

---

## Takeaways

1. For LLM traffic, the load balancer has to understand the model server. Queue depth and KV-cache state matter more than connection counts.
2. Prefix-cache affinity is the cheapest performance win available — as long as you guard against hot spots.
3. Gateway API's inference extension is turning these ideas into a standard Kubernetes API, so model-aware routing no longer needs a bespoke proxy.

title: Sidecar-less Service Mesh: Ambient Mode, eBPF and the Gateway API
excerpt: Why meshes are dropping per-pod sidecars for node-level L4 proxies, optional L7 waypoints and eBPF — and how Gateway API makes the mesh swappable.
content:
## Why sidecars are being retired

The classic service-mesh design injects an Envoy sidecar into every pod. It gave us mTLS, retries and traffic splitting without touching application code — and it also gave us:

- a proxy's worth of CPU and memory **per pod**, multiplied across thousands of pods;
- restarts of every workload to upgrade the mesh;
- startup races where the app tries to talk before its sidecar is ready;
- full L7 parsing cost even for services that only needed encryption.

The industry's answer over the last two years has been the **sidecar-less mesh**: split the data plane into a cheap, always-on L4 layer and an optional L7 layer you pay for only where you need it.

```text
 Sidecar model                      Ambient / node-level model
 ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐          ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
 │ app│envoy│ │ app│envoy│          │ app  │ │ app  │ │ app  │
 └──────────┘ └──────────┘          └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘
   N pods = N proxies                  └── per-node L4 proxy ──┘
                                            │  (mTLS, identity)
                                            ▼
                                     optional L7 waypoint
                                     (only for services that need it)
```

---

## 1. Istio ambient mode

Istio's ambient mode, generally available since Istio 1.24, is the clearest example of the split:

- **ztunnel** runs once per node (written in Rust). It handles L4: workload identity, mTLS and L4 authorization. Traffic between nodes is tunnelled over **HBONE** — HTTP/2 `CONNECT` on port 15008.
- **Waypoint proxies** are Envoy deployments you opt into per namespace or service when you need L7 features: header-based routing, retries, L7 authorization.

Enrolling a namespace is a label, not a redeploy:

```bash
kubectl label namespace shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
# only if you need L7 policy for this namespace:
istioctl waypoint apply -n shop --enroll-namespace
```

That last point is the real win: most services only need encryption and identity, so most services never pay for an L7 proxy.

---

## 2. eBPF moves work into the kernel

Cilium takes the node-level idea further by doing as much as possible in **eBPF** — programs attached to kernel hooks that can route, load-balance and enforce policy on packets without bouncing them through a user-space proxy. When L7 is needed, it hands traffic to a per-node Envoy.

The trade-off worth understanding: eBPF is extremely fast for L3/L4 decisions, but parsing HTTP/2 or gRPC still belongs in a real proxy. Good designs push the cheap decisions down and keep the expensive ones optional.

---

## 3. One API to configure it all: Gateway API (and GAMMA)

The other quiet revolution is configuration. Every mesh used to ship its own CRDs. **Gateway API** — GA since v1.0 — standardises routing, and the **GAMMA** initiative extends the same resources to east-west mesh traffic by attaching an `HTTPRoute` directly to a `Service`:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: checkout-canary
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - group: ""
    kind: Service
    name: checkout          # mesh traffic to this Service...
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: checkout-v1
      port: 8080
      weight: 90
    - name: checkout-v2     # ...gets a 10% canary
      port: 8080
      weight: 10
```

The same manifest works across conformant implementations, which makes the mesh a swappable component instead of a lock-in decision.

---

## 4. Where cloud-native management fits

With meshes, gateways and policies all expressed as Kubernetes resources, the hard part shifts from *installing* infrastructure to *understanding and changing it safely*. That's the space Meshery — the CNCF cloud-native manager I contribute to — works in: modelling infrastructure as visual, versionable designs, validating relationships between components, and deploying them consistently across clusters. My own contributions there have been on the Go server side, for example making environment lookups ignore soft-deleted connections so the UI never shows infrastructure that no longer exists.

---

## Choosing in practice

1. **Only need mTLS and identity?** A node-level L4 data plane (ambient ztunnel, or Cilium) gives you most of the value at a fraction of the cost.
2. **Need canaries, retries, header routing?** Add L7 — but only to the services that need it (waypoints, or per-node Envoy).
3. **Write routes in Gateway API.** It keeps your options open if you change mesh later.
4. **Measure before and after.** Per-pod memory, p99 latency and mesh upgrade time are the three numbers that justify the migration.

title: Gang Scheduling Meets DRA: Kubernetes as a Scheduler for AI Workloads
excerpt: All-or-nothing placement with Volcano and Kueue, Dynamic Resource Allocation for GPUs, and topology-aware scheduling — lessons from working in a scheduler codebase.
content:
## The problem: Kubernetes was built to place pods, not jobs

The default Kubernetes scheduler makes one decision at a time: take a pending pod, find a node that fits, bind it, move on. That works beautifully for stateless web services. It falls apart for the workloads that now dominate cluster spend — distributed training and large batch jobs — where a job is only useful if **all** of its workers run at the same time.

Picture a 16-worker training job on a cluster with room for 12 GPUs. Pod-by-pod scheduling happily starts 12 workers, which then sit idle waiting for peers that will never arrive. Worse, a second job does the same with the remaining capacity, and now two jobs are deadlocked holding resources neither can use.

```text
  Job A (needs 16) ──► 12 running, 4 pending   ✗ stuck, burning GPUs
  Job B (needs 8)  ──►  0 running, 8 pending   ✗ starved
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Gang scheduling:     A waits whole, B runs whole  ✓ cluster does useful work
```

Two shifts are fixing this at the platform level: **gang scheduling** and **Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA)**.

---

## 1. Gang scheduling: all or nothing

Gang scheduling treats a group of pods as one unit. Either the scheduler can place the minimum number of members together, or it places none of them and keeps the capacity free for something that fits.

In Volcano (a CNCF project I contribute to), the unit is a `PodGroup` with a `minMember`:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: llm-finetune
spec:
  minMember: 16          # don't start anything until 16 can start
  queue: research
  minResources:
    cpu: "64"
```

Internally Volcano runs a pipeline of **actions** each scheduling cycle — `enqueue`, `allocate`, `preempt`, `reclaim`, `backfill` — and **plugins** such as `gang`, `drf`, `proportion`, `priority` and `binpack` vote on every decision. The `gang` plugin is what refuses to commit a partial allocation; `proportion` and queues make sure one team can't starve another.

Kueue, from the Kubernetes SIGs, approaches the same problem from the admission side: jobs wait in queues against quotas and are only admitted when their whole footprint fits. The two ideas are complementary — admission control decides *whether* a job may start, gang-aware scheduling decides *where* its pods land.

---

## 2. DRA: devices stop being opaque counters

For years GPUs were requested as an extended resource:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

That's just an integer. The scheduler can't tell an 80 GB card from a 24 GB one, can't express "two GPUs on the same NVLink island", and can't share a device between containers cleanly.

**Dynamic Resource Allocation** replaces the counter with a real API. Drivers publish devices and their attributes as `ResourceSlice`s; admins define `DeviceClass`es; workloads ask for devices through `ResourceClaim`s with CEL selectors. DRA's core graduated to stable in Kubernetes 1.34, which is why you're now seeing it in managed clusters.

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: big-gpu
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu
        exactly:
          deviceClassName: gpu.example.com
          selectors:
          - cel:
              expression: >-
                device.capacity["gpu.example.com"].memory
                  .compareTo(quantity("40Gi")) >= 0
```

The pod then references the claim instead of a magic resource name. Because the scheduler now understands device attributes, it can make placement decisions that used to live in vendor-specific device plugins.

---

## 3. Topology is the next frontier

Once you place jobs as a whole, the next question is *how close* their members are. All-reduce traffic between training workers is brutal; two workers on the same rack switch can be dramatically faster than two workers three hops apart. Recent Volcano releases add network-topology-aware scheduling, modelling racks and switches as a hierarchy so a gang lands inside the tightest network tier that can hold it.

```text
          spine
         /     \
     leaf-1   leaf-2        ← prefer: whole gang under one leaf
     /  \      /  \
   n1   n2   n3   n4
```

---

## What working in a scheduler codebase taught me

- **Correctness beats cleverness.** A scheduler that occasionally commits a partial gang is worse than a slow one. Most bugs I've seen are in edge cases — preemption racing with a job that just became ready, or caches drifting from the API server.
- **Tests need realistic fixtures.** I spent time separating E2E fixtures from examples in Volcano's test suite; it's unglamorous, but it's what makes refactors of scheduling workflows safe.
- **Every cycle is a budget.** Plugins run for every pending job on every cycle. An `O(n²)` helper is invisible on a laptop and painful at a few thousand nodes.

---

## Takeaways

1. If your cluster runs multi-pod jobs, pod-at-a-time scheduling is quietly wasting capacity. Add gang semantics (Volcano) or gang-aware admission (Kueue).
2. Plan the move from `nvidia.com/gpu: N` to DRA claims — it unlocks attribute-based selection and sharing.
3. Watch topology-aware placement: for distributed training it's the difference between buying more GPUs and using the ones you have.
